problems.source_says: Table 2 counts the logged corpus: 460 treatment ideas include 373 AI-origin suggestions and 87 human-origin ideas. Section 4.1 separately identifies only 115 accepted/copied AI suggestions, and section 3.1 explicitly excludes unaccepted AI suggestions from participants' results. The form accurately describes this distinction, but its fluency/participant-output coding is not supported for the full-log total: the codebook defines fluency as the number of ideas a person produces. This is a descriptive corpus count that includes model suggestions not incorporated into participant output; it should not be treated as a criterion-3 participant-output fluency score. The category_count measure and set unit are appropriate for the logged corpus itself.
problems.quote: only suggestions in the “list of ideas” (left side of the screen) would count toward their results (i.e., not-accepted AI ideas are excluded).
problems.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), section 3.1, final paragraph; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Table 2; PDF pp. 5–6 (printed pp. 425–426), section 4.1, accepted/copied subset. Codebook sections 3 (criterion 3) and 6 (fluency).

problems.source_says: This analysis uses contributions produced within human+AI brainstorming sessions, while AI was available. It counts new-category contributions within a session, not diversity across different people. With ai_available_when_produced=yes and construct=other, the codebook rule requires question=with_ai. Its descriptive, within-arm comparison does not provide an exception to that question-assignment rule; it can remain explicitly identified as a nonrandomized source/process comparison.
problems.quote: This analysis can only be carried out for the human+AI condition.
problems.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 427), section 4.2, paragraph beginning "We thus additionally take a process perspective"; codebook section 1, final question-assignment sentence (line 17).
